learningGoal.source: Explain how AI can make realistic pictures, videos and voices, tell labelled creative work from a fake, and check the source before you trust or share one.

read.sections.0.heading.source: AI can make pictures, videos and voices
read.sections.0.heading.back: AI can produce pictures, videos and voices

read.sections.0.text.source: Some AI tools can create new pictures, videos and voices. These tools learned from enormous numbers of real examples, so what they make can look and sound realistic. Many people use these tools openly and creatively. Artists make pictures, film makers add effects and teachers make lessons, and they say that AI helped. In Greenhill, the comedy club posted a talking goat with the label “Made with AI, just for fun”, so that is not a trick. A fake is different: it pretends to show something real that never happened. A deepfake is a fake that copies a real person's face or voice, often to trick people for money or attention. Labels can get lost, too. If someone shares the goat video without its label, as if it were real, it can mislead people.
read.sections.0.text.back: Some AI tools can create new pictures, videos and voices. These tools learned from a huge number of real examples, so what they produce can look and sound realistic. Many people use these tools openly and creatively. Artists make pictures, film makers add special effects and teachers prepare lessons, and they say that AI helped. In Greenhill, the comedy club posted a talking goat with the label “Made with AI, just for fun”, so that is not a trick. Fake content is different: it pretends to show something real that never happened. A deepfake is fake content that copies a real person's face or voice, often to trick people for money or attention. Labels can also get lost. If someone shares the goat video without its label, as if it were real, the video can mislead people.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Trick" is "helah"; "a fake" stays "kandungan palsu" (fake content), as in the rest of the lesson.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Strange details are clues, not proof
read.sections.1.heading.back: Strange details are clues, not proof

read.sections.1.text.source: AI pictures sometimes have small mistakes, such as an extra finger, messy letters on a sign or a background that melts into a wall. In a video, the mouth may not move with the words. These details can be clues, but they are not proof. Newer tools make fewer mistakes, so a fake can look perfect. Real photographs can also look strange, for example when they are blurry or taken in poor light. In a 2025 study by researchers in the United States, more than 50,000 people judged real photos and AI pictures online. They wrongly called about one in four real photos AI-made, and they also missed about one in four AI pictures. The fruit seller's photo has very smooth skin, but the photo club says who took it, with a phone.
read.sections.1.text.back: AI pictures sometimes have small mistakes, such as an extra finger, messy letters on a sign or a background that seems to melt into a wall. In a video, the mouth may not move with the words. These details can be clues, but not proof. Newer tools make fewer mistakes, so fake content can look perfect. Real photos can also look strange, for example when the photo is blurry or taken in dim light. In a 2025 study by researchers in the United States, more than 50,000 people judged real photos and AI pictures online. They wrongly called about one in four real photos AI-made, and they also failed to spot about one in four AI pictures. The fruit seller's photo shows very smooth skin, but the photo club says who took it, with a phone.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Missed" is "tidak dapat mengesan" (could not detect). Check "menyatakan siapa yang mengambilnya, dengan telefon" reads naturally.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: AI pictures sometimes have mistakes, like six fingers or messy letters. These are clues. But clues are not proof. New tools make fewer mistakes. read.sections.1.simpler.back: AI pictures sometimes have mistakes, like six fingers or messy letters. These are clues. But clues are not proof. New tools make fewer mistakes. People thought about one in four real photos were AI-made. They also did not notice about one in four AI pictures. The fruit seller has very smooth skin. But the photo club says a phone took that photo.

read.sections.2.text.source: So the most useful check is the source. Who posted it, and when? Can you find where it first came from, and does the maker say how it was made? Do other trusted sources show the same thing? Make sure they did not all copy one post, because ten copies are still one source. Fact-checking groups do this work for pictures that spread widely. In Greenhill, the farm's own page says it grew no giant pumpkin, and a page with no name posted the photo. So that photo is probably fake. For a voice message, contact the person in another way. Coach Ana's message came from an unknown number, so ask her in person. If you still can't tell, say so, and don't share it yet.
read.sections.2.text.back: So the most useful check is its source. Who posted it, and when? Can you find where it first came from, and does its maker say how it was made? Do other trusted sources show the same thing? Make sure they did not all copy the same one post, because ten copies are still one source. Fact-checking groups do this work for pictures that spread widely. In Greenhill, the farm's own page says the farm did not grow a giant pumpkin, and a page with no name posted the photo. So the photo is probably fake. For a voice message, contact the person in another way. Coach Ana's message came from an unknown number, so ask her in person. If you are still not sure, say so, and don't share it yet.

watch.summary.source: This video comes from a series made with a team of teenage fact-checkers. It explains that some people use AI to make fake pictures, videos and sounds. They often do it to get money, attention or power. The video shows clues to look for. AI pictures can have strange hands, odd shadows and strange backgrounds. In AI videos, look for edges that blur or flicker. Check the shadows, and check if the lips move with the words. For AI voices, listen to the tone and to the sounds in the background. The video also shows tools that can help, like a search that finds where else a picture appears online. But these tools are not always right. A person still needs to think and check before sharing.
watch.summary.back: This video is from a series made together with a team of teenage fact-checkers. This video explains that some people use AI to produce fake pictures, videos and sounds. They often do it to get money, attention or power. This video shows clues to look for. AI pictures may have strange hands, odd shadows and strange backgrounds. In AI videos, look for edges that blur or flicker. Check the shadows, and check whether the lips move with the words. For AI voices, listen to the tone and the sounds in the background. This video also shows tools that can help, such as a search that finds other places the picture appears online. But these tools are not always right. A human still needs to think and check before sharing it.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Deepfakes are used to hurt real people: fake pictures that shame someone, fake videos of leaders, and cloned voices in scams (for example a call that sounds like a relative asking for money; see the FTC source). The lesson keeps its examples silly on purpose. Don't show real deepfakes of real people in class. If a learner says a fake was made of them or someone they know, don't discuss the details in class; follow the partner's own safeguarding process.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Deepfakes are used to hurt real people: fake pictures that shame someone, fake videos of leaders, and cloned voices in scams (for example a call that sounds like a relative asking for money; see the FTC source). This lesson keeps its examples funny on purpose. Do not show real deepfakes of real people in class. If a learner says fake content has been made about them or someone they know, do not discuss the details in class; follow the partner organisation's own child safeguarding process.

educatorNotes.0.source: Teach checking first: who posted it, when, where it first came from, whether the maker says how it was made, whether other trusted sources show the same thing (and didn't all copy one post), and for a voice, contacting the person another way. Visual glitches (extra fingers, messy letters, smooth skin) are reasons to check, never proof: newer tools make fewer of them, and real photos can show odd details too. The study in section 2 is Kamali and others (CHI '25, Northwestern University): more than 50,000 online participants judged 450 AI-made and 149 real images; they called real photographs real in 74% of observations and AI-made images AI-made in 76%, so about one in four was misjudged each way. It is one online study with the authors' own image set, not a general rate. Accept “can't tell yet” as a strong answer. On paper, read the four Greenhill posts aloud and discuss what each source tells you; there is no sorting task.
educatorNotes.0.back: Teach checking first: who posted it, when, where it first came from, whether its maker says how it was made, whether other trusted sources show the same thing (and did not all copy one post), and for a voice, contacting the person another way. Visual glitches (extra fingers, messy letters, smooth skin) are reasons to check, never proof: newer tools produce fewer glitches, and real photos can show odd details too. The study in part 2 is Kamali and colleagues (CHI '25, Northwestern University): more than 50,000 online participants judged 450 AI-made and 149 real images; they called real photos real in 74% of observations and AI-made images AI-made in 76%, so about one in four was misjudged for each kind. It is one online study with the authors' own image set, not a general rate. Accept “can't tell yet” as a strong answer. On paper, read the four Greenhill posts aloud and discuss what each source tells you; there is no sorting task.

educatorNotes.1.source: Labelled AI work (art, film effects, lessons, a joke clearly marked “Made with AI”) is not the same as a fake that pretends to be real or copies a real person. Labels can be lost when a picture is reposted (News Literacy Project, 2026), so a labelled post can become misleading when shared without it. In Indonesia, Mafindo's TurnBackHoax and CekFakta check viral pictures and videos, and Mafindo says AI-based hoaxes are getting harder to tell apart (Liputan6, 2026). A teacher with internet can show one checked example; learners don't need to go online.
educatorNotes.1.back: Labelled AI work (art, special effects in films, lessons, a joke clearly marked “Made with AI”) is not the same as fake content that pretends to be real or copies a real person. In Indonesia, Mafindo's TurnBackHoax and CekFakta check viral pictures and videos, and Mafindo says AI-based fake news is getting harder to tell apart (Liputan6, 2026). A teacher with internet can show one checked example; learners don't need to go online.
